items.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007
items.q: I think Buddy DeFranco for instance has warmed up a lot. About ten years ago I heard somebody say hey, that’s really — I hear he is sort of phenomenal you know. But I didn’t get much warmth out of him.

ctx.x: Well I’m curious, how do you explain to someone who is only familiar with jazz in the big sense, well what’s traditional jazz as opposed to modern jazz?

Okay Monk, you hit the nail — I’ve been working for years, I’ve got about 30 chapters in the computers about Louis Armstrong. And it’s very rarely discussed. It’s a very big problem of the music and it doesn’t get discussed much — what is jazz? And it’s a very difficult subject, and how do you define what is jazz. And I’ve tried, well it’s swing. Well no, a lot of music swings. It’s got soul, whatever. A lot of music has got soul. It’s got to have — I think it’s got to be a strong touch of the blues, some of the…

Because most stuff that passes for jazz today I do not care for. I don’t like it. And they’ve got a perfect right, they’ve got a right to play them blues but it doesn’t interest me. Okay. So it boils down to what is jazz? It’s got to have some blue notes, it’s got to swing, it’s got to be — it helps if it’s original. It’s sort of life generally it’s got to be in a certain bag, you know what I mean? A certain form, bebop or whatever, however. But it’s very hard to define. And I thought about it and thought about…
